# Brave New Hive

> A marketing pedia for brands in the age of AI. The Hive is where the knowledge is kept. brave-new.com is where it gets used.

Full text of every entry. Published by Brave New (https://brave-new.com). Every entry is dated, sourced and signed by the Brave New team.

## 01 Principles

The handful of ideas most marketing still rests on, each with the person and the year it came from.

### The 4 Ps of marketing

Source: https://bravenewhive.com/principles/4-ps-of-marketing/
Date: 2026-09-08. Read: 3 min.

Product, price, place, promotion. E. Jerome McCarthy set the frame out in Basic Marketing in 1960, and it is still the first thing most marketers learn.

E. Jerome McCarthy published Basic Marketing: A Managerial Approach in 1960. The book reduced the marketing mix to four decisions: what you sell, what you charge, where it can be bought, and how people hear about it.

The frame is old and it shows. It says nothing about what the brand means in the buyer's head, which is where the next entries pick up.

### Positioning in marketing

Source: https://bravenewhive.com/principles/positioning-in-marketing/
Date: 2026-09-05. Read: 4 min.

Al Ries and Jack Trout argued in 1972 that a brand is a position in the prospect's mind, not a list of features. The book followed in 1981.

Ries and Trout first published the idea as a series of articles in Advertising Age in 1972, then as Positioning: The Battle for Your Mind in 1981.

The claim is simple. The mind is crowded, it accepts only what fits what it already knows, and the job is to own a word before a competitor does. Most positioning statements still describe the company rather than the space it wants to hold.

### Market segmentation

Source: https://bravenewhive.com/principles/market-segmentation/
Date: 2026-09-01. Read: 3 min.

Wendell Smith's 1956 paper in the Journal of Marketing separated product differentiation from market segmentation. Marketing has been splitting audiences ever since.

Wendell R. Smith published Product Differentiation and Market Segmentation as Alternative Marketing Strategies in the Journal of Marketing in 1956.

The idea: a market is not one demand curve but several, so a company can serve a slice on its own terms rather than the whole on average terms. The hard part is choosing what to leave out.

### Unique selling proposition (USP)

Source: https://bravenewhive.com/principles/unique-selling-proposition/
Date: 2026-08-27. Read: 3 min.

Rosser Reeves, Reality in Advertising, 1961. Every ad must make a proposition the competition cannot or does not make, and it must be strong enough to move people.

Rosser Reeves of Ted Bates & Company codified the USP in Reality in Advertising (1961). Three conditions: the ad proposes a specific benefit, the proposition is one competitors do not offer, and it is strong enough to pull new customers.

Reeves wrote for a world of repetition on three television networks. The discipline of one claim, stated plainly, survived the medium.

### Mental availability and physical availability

Source: https://bravenewhive.com/principles/mental-and-physical-availability/
Date: 2026-08-22. Read: 4 min.

Byron Sharp's How Brands Grow (2010) argued brands grow by being easy to think of and easy to buy, not by deepening loyalty among a few.

Byron Sharp and the Ehrenberg-Bass Institute published How Brands Grow in 2010. The evidence base is buying data across categories and decades.

Mental availability is the chance a brand comes to mind in a buying situation. Physical availability is the ease of buying it when the moment comes. Distinctive assets, reach and consistency do most of the work. Duller than most marketers want, and what the data keeps giving.

### The Long and the Short of It

Source: https://bravenewhive.com/principles/the-long-and-the-short-of-it/
Date: 2026-08-18. Read: 4 min.

Les Binet and Peter Field, IPA, 2013. Brand building and sales activation work on different timescales, and the mix most often cited is roughly 60 to 40.

Binet and Field analysed the IPA Effectiveness Databank and published The Long and the Short of It in 2013.

Activation produces quick sales spikes that fade. Brand building works slowly and compounds. Campaigns doing both outperformed campaigns doing either alone. Everyone quotes the split. Fewer budgets show it.

### AIDA

Source: https://bravenewhive.com/principles/aida/
Date: 2026-08-12. Read: 2 min.

Attention, interest, desire, action. The sequence is usually attributed to the American advertising writer E. St. Elmo Lewis in the late 1890s.

The model describes the steps a message has to move a person through before they buy. Attribution is messier than the acronym suggests. Lewis is the usual name, writing in the late 1890s, but the record does not settle cleanly on one author.

It remains the skeleton under most funnels, landing pages and sales decks, whether or not the people using it know its name.

### Brand equity

Source: https://bravenewhive.com/principles/brand-equity/
Date: 2026-08-06. Read: 3 min.

David Aaker's Managing Brand Equity (1991) and Kevin Lane Keller's customer-based brand equity (1993) gave the value of a name a structure you can measure.

Aaker's 1991 book set out brand equity as a set of assets: awareness, associations, perceived quality, loyalty. Keller's 1993 paper in the Journal of Marketing framed it from the customer side, as the effect brand knowledge has on the response to marketing.

Both made the same point to finance departments: a brand is an asset that produces cash flows, and it can be built or wasted.

## 02 History of advertising

A timeline of the moments that changed how advertising and marketing reach people, from the first agency to the first AI answer. Who invented advertising, when the first commercials ran, and what each change did.

### 1841. Who invented the advertising agency

Source: https://bravenewhive.com/history-of-advertising/1841-who-invented-the-advertising-agency/
Date: 2026-09-07. Read: 2 min.

Volney B. Palmer opened what is generally regarded as the first advertising agency in the United States, in Philadelphia, selling newspaper space on commission.

Palmer acted as a broker between newspapers and advertisers. The commission that paid him set the agency model, and the question that came with it: whose side is the agency on.

### 1922. The first paid radio commercial

Source: https://bravenewhive.com/history-of-advertising/1922-the-first-radio-commercial/
Date: 2026-09-03. Read: 2 min.

On 28 August 1922, WEAF in New York aired a ten-minute talk paid for by the Queensboro Corporation to sell apartments in Jackson Heights.

The spot was closer to a sponsored lecture than to a jingle. It established that broadcast time could be sold, which financed everything radio and television did afterwards.

### 1941. The first television commercial

Source: https://bravenewhive.com/history-of-advertising/1941-the-first-television-commercial/
Date: 2026-08-29. Read: 2 min.

On 1 July 1941, a Bulova watch spot ran on WNBT New York before a Dodgers and Phillies game. It showed a clock face and a short line of copy.

The commercial lasted about ten seconds. We keep coming back to that. The medium that shaped the second half of the century starts as a time check.

### 1960. The 4 Ps of marketing are published

Source: https://bravenewhive.com/history-of-advertising/1960-the-four-ps/
Date: 2026-08-24. Read: 2 min.

E. Jerome McCarthy's Basic Marketing gave marketing its first widely taught framework.

See the Principles entry on the 4 Ps for the frame itself. Its place in the timeline matters because it turned marketing from a trade into a subject.

### 1972. The Positioning Era Cometh

Source: https://bravenewhive.com/history-of-advertising/1972-the-positioning-era/
Date: 2026-08-19. Read: 2 min.

Ries and Trout's series in Advertising Age moved the battleground from the product to the prospect's mind.

The articles argued that product-led and image-led advertising had run out of road, and that the winning move was to occupy a position the competition had left open. Nothing since has made the market less crowded.

### 1994. The first banner ad

Source: https://bravenewhive.com/history-of-advertising/1994-the-first-banner-ad/
Date: 2026-08-14. Read: 2 min.

On 27 October 1994, HotWired ran a banner for AT&T. Digital advertising began as a rectangle at the top of a page.

The ad asked whether the reader had ever clicked their mouse right here, and told them they would. Click-through rates for that first campaign are widely reported to have been far above anything the format achieved later. The figure gets repeated more often than it gets sourced.

### 2000. Google launches AdWords

Source: https://bravenewhive.com/history-of-advertising/2000-google-adwords/
Date: 2026-08-09. Read: 2 min.

In October 2000, Google opened self-service search advertising. The ad was matched to the search query. Intent became something a marketer could buy.

AdWords tied the ad to the search query. Pricing per click followed in 2002. Small budgets became viable and measurement became standard, and for two decades the results page was the most valuable real estate in marketing. That run is ending.

### 2022. ChatGPT is released

Source: https://bravenewhive.com/history-of-advertising/2022-chatgpt/
Date: 2026-08-04. Read: 3 min.

OpenAI released ChatGPT on 30 November 2022. Within months, a growing share of buyers were asking a model for a recommendation instead of reading a results page.

The shift changes what a brand has to be. A results page ranks ten options. An answer names one or two, and eleventh is the same as absent. Whether a model can retrieve a brand, and describe it correctly, is now a marketing question rather than a technical one. The AI marketing section is about that.

## 03 Branding

How brands are built and how the brain receives them: brand strategy, brand equity, and the neuromarketing studies that are documented.

### The Coke and Pepsi brain study (the Pepsi paradox)

Source: https://bravenewhive.com/branding/the-coke-pepsi-study/
Date: 2026-09-06. Read: 4 min.

McClure and colleagues, Neuron, 2004. Told which cola they were drinking, people's stated preference and their brain activity both changed. The brand did the work the taste did not.

The study, from Read Montague's lab at Baylor College of Medicine, ran blind and labelled taste tests inside an fMRI scanner. In the blind condition preferences split. With the Coke label visible, preference shifted toward Coke and activity changed in regions associated with memory and self-image.

It is the most cited demonstration that a brand is a stored pattern in the buyer, not a property of the product.

### System 1 and System 2 thinking in marketing

Source: https://bravenewhive.com/branding/system-1-and-system-2/
Date: 2026-09-02. Read: 3 min.

Daniel Kahneman, Thinking, Fast and Slow, 2011. Most decisions, including most purchases, run on the fast, automatic system, and the slow one mostly rationalises afterwards.

Kahneman's book summarised decades of research with Amos Tversky. System 1 is fast, associative and effortless. System 2 is slow, deliberate and lazy.

For a brand the implication is blunt. What feels familiar is decided before the argument is heard. The argument arrives later, to justify it.

### The somatic marker hypothesis

Source: https://bravenewhive.com/branding/somatic-markers/
Date: 2026-08-26. Read: 3 min.

Antonio Damasio, Descartes' Error, 1994. Emotion is part of the machinery of choosing, not noise laid over reason. Patients who lost it could not decide.

Damasio studied patients with damage to the ventromedial prefrontal cortex. Their reasoning was intact and their decision making collapsed. His explanation: the body's emotional signals mark options as good or bad before deliberation starts.

Advertising that produces a feeling is making the argument in the channel the brain uses.

### Where the word came from

Source: https://bravenewhive.com/branding/where-the-word-came-from/
Date: 2026-08-20. Read: 2 min.

The term neuromarketing is commonly credited to Ale Smidts of Erasmus University in Rotterdam, in 2002.

The field grew out of consumer neuroscience in the early 2000s, when brain imaging became cheap enough to point at advertising. Much of what has been sold under the label since is thinner than the founding studies. This section sticks to the documented ones.

### Processing fluency in marketing

Source: https://bravenewhive.com/branding/processing-fluency-in-marketing/
Date: 2026-08-15. Read: 3 min.

Things that are easy to read, see and say are judged more true and more likeable. Reber, Schwarz and Winkielman set the effect out in 2004.

The ease with which the brain processes a stimulus is itself read as a signal. Clear names, legible type, repeated shapes and short claims feel more true than the same content made harder. The brain is grading the effort, not the content.

It is the scientific case for consistency, and against cleverness that costs the reader effort.

### Loss aversion in marketing

Source: https://bravenewhive.com/branding/loss-aversion-in-marketing/
Date: 2026-08-10. Read: 3 min.

Kahneman and Tversky's prospect theory, 1979. Losses weigh roughly twice as much as gains of the same size. Most urgency in marketing borrows from this.

Prospect Theory: An Analysis of Decision under Risk was published in Econometrica in 1979. The asymmetry it describes underlies deadlines, free trials that expire and the framing of what a buyer stands to lose by not acting.

Used honestly it clarifies stakes. Used carelessly it trains people to distrust the brand.

## 04 AI marketing

What AI marketing, AI SEO, generative engine optimization and answer engine optimization mean, and what changes for a brand when the buyer asks a model instead of a search engine.

### What is AI marketing?

Source: https://bravenewhive.com/ai-marketing/what-is-ai-marketing/
Date: 2026-09-14. Read: 3 min.

AI marketing is the use of AI systems in marketing work: to research buyers, generate and test creative, target and bid, and to earn a place in the answers AI assistants give when buyers ask for a recommendation.

The phrase covers two different jobs that often get mixed together. The first is using AI inside the marketing team: research, drafting, audience models, bidding, personalisation, reporting. The second is marketing to AI: making sure the systems buyers now ask can find the company, name it and describe it correctly.

The second job is the newer one. ChatGPT was released on 30 November 2022, and asking a model for a shortlist has since become a normal step before a purchase. That step happens before the buyer reaches anyone's website, which is why it belongs to marketing rather than to a tools budget.

Most of what is sold as AI marketing is the first job. Most of what changes a company's pipeline is the second. The entries in this section cover the terms used for it: AI SEO, generative engine optimization, answer engine optimization, and retrievable brands.

### What is generative engine optimization (GEO)?

Source: https://bravenewhive.com/ai-marketing/what-is-generative-engine-optimization/
Date: 2026-09-13. Read: 3 min.

Generative engine optimization, or GEO, is the practice of writing and structuring content so that generative engines cite it in the answers they produce. The term comes from a 2023 research paper by Pranjal Aggarwal and colleagues.

The paper, GEO: Generative Engine Optimization, was posted to arXiv in November 2023 by Pranjal Aggarwal, Vishvak Murahari, Tanmay Rajpurohit, Ashwin Kalyan, Karthik Narasimhan and Ameet Deshpande. It introduced the term and a benchmark for testing which changes to a source make it more likely to be used in a generated answer. The authors reported visibility gains of up to 40 per cent on that benchmark.

The practical reading: a generative engine assembles an answer and decides which sources to lean on, instead of ranking pages for a click. So write the sentence you want quoted, put the source next to it, and stop optimising for a position the answer never shows.attributes it, and puts a quotable sentence next to a source gives the engine something it can reuse.

GEO overlaps with SEO at the base, because a page still has to be reachable and readable. It separates on the goal: a position in a list, or a sentence in an answer.

### What is answer engine optimization (AEO)?

Source: https://bravenewhive.com/ai-marketing/what-is-answer-engine-optimization/
Date: 2026-09-11. Read: 3 min.

Answer engine optimization, or AEO, is the practice of preparing content so that it is used in a direct answer rather than a list of links. In practice it means answering one question per page, plainly and early.

AEO grew out of the years when search engines began answering questions on the results page itself, through featured snippets and knowledge panels. Publishers learned one habit from that period: one question, one clear answer, one page. It transferred to AI assistants without much translation.one clear answer per page, transferred straight to AI assistants.

The mechanics are unglamorous. Use the question as the heading, in the words people type. Answer it in the first two or three sentences. Keep the answer self-contained so it still makes sense when it is lifted out of the page. Put a date, an author and a source on it.

AEO and GEO are now used almost interchangeably. Where people separate them, AEO is about the direct answer and GEO about the generated one. The work is the same work.

### What is AI SEO?

Source: https://bravenewhive.com/ai-marketing/what-is-ai-seo/
Date: 2026-09-10. Read: 3 min.

AI SEO means two things: using AI tools to do SEO work faster, and optimising a site so that AI search features and assistants surface it. The second is the one that decides whether a brand appears in an answer.

The first meaning is a workflow question. Keyword clustering, drafting, internal linking and schema generation done with AI assistance. It saves hours and changes nothing about what a site deserves to be returned for.

The second meaning is the strategic one. Search results now carry AI-generated summaries above the links, and some buyers ask an assistant instead of opening a results page at all. Being in the ten blue links and being in the summary above them are two different outcomes.

What serves the second meaning: pages built around one question, definitions placed early, structured data, a visible author and date, and a company description that reads the same everywhere it appears. None of that is new SEO advice. It matters more when the output is one paragraph instead of ten links.

### What is a retrievable brand?

Source: https://bravenewhive.com/ai-marketing/what-is-a-retrievable-brand/
Date: 2026-09-08. Read: 3 min.

A retrievable brand is one that AI assistants and search engines can find, name and describe correctly when a buyer asks. It is built from clear definitions, named frameworks, sourced facts and one consistent description repeated everywhere.

A model answering a question about a category assembles what it can retrieve about each company: the site, the listings, the coverage, the profiles. Contradictions between those sources do not rank lower. They get averaged into something vague, or dropped.

Retrievability is a term from information retrieval, the research field behind search engines, for how easily a document can be surfaced by a system. Leif Azzopardi and Vishwa Vinay proposed it as a measure in 2008. Applied to a brand it asks a blunter question: when a buyer asks for the category, does the name come back.

Brave New, which publishes the Hive, uses retrievable brand as the name of its method. The pillars are short: one definition repeated word for word, a named framework the model can attribute, sourced claims, a visible author and date, and machine-readable structure.

### How do AI models choose which brands to recommend?

Source: https://bravenewhive.com/ai-marketing/how-ai-models-choose-brands/
Date: 2026-09-06. Read: 4 min.

Models answer from what they were trained on and what they can retrieve at the moment of the question. A brand gets named when it is described the same way across many independent sources and is easy to quote.

Nobody outside the providers can see the weighting, and they do not publish it. What is observable is the pattern in the answers: the brands that come back are described the same way in many places, by sources the system treats as reliable. That is inference rather than documentation, and it is worth saying so.consistently in many places, by sources the system treats as reliable.

Two mechanisms are at work. Training gives the model a rough map of a category from what was on the public web when it was built. Retrieval at question time pulls current pages and cites them. A brand missing from both is not in the running.

The practical consequence is that third-party coverage does more work than site copy. A company can call itself the leading provider on its own homepage as often as it likes. The model is counting how many other sources put it in that category.

It also explains why a rebrand or a change of category costs more than it used to. The old description stays on the web, and it keeps being counted.

### How do I get my company mentioned in ChatGPT and Perplexity answers?

Source: https://bravenewhive.com/ai-marketing/get-mentioned-in-chatgpt-and-perplexity/
Date: 2026-09-04. Read: 4 min.

Publish a plain definition of what you do, keep that description identical everywhere it appears, earn coverage on the sources the engines already cite, and make your pages easy to read, date and attribute. Then check the answers monthly.

Start by finding out what the engines say now. Write down the ten questions a buyer would actually type, ask each engine, and record three things: whether you are named, where in the answer, and whether the description is right. That is the baseline, and it takes an afternoon.

Then look at what the answers cite. The sources that keep appearing for your category are the ones worth being in: trade publications, directories, association pages, well-kept reference sites. Being described correctly there moves the answer more than another post on your own blog.

On your own site the work is mechanical. One question per page. The answer in the first sixty words. A visible author and date. Schema markup. The same company description in every profile, listing and bio you control.

Then repeat the check on a fixed schedule. Answers move as the sources move, and a single reading tells you nothing about direction.

### What is llms.txt?

Source: https://bravenewhive.com/ai-marketing/what-is-llms-txt/
Date: 2026-09-03. Read: 2 min.

llms.txt is a plain text file placed at the root of a website that gives AI systems a short, curated summary of the site and links to its most useful pages. Jeremy Howard of Answer.AI proposed it in 2024.

The reasoning behind the proposal: a model reading a web page has a limited context window and has to wade through navigation, scripts and styling to reach the content. A markdown file at /llms.txt hands it the short version instead.

The format is simple. The site name as a heading, a short description, then linked sections with a line of context for each. Some sites also publish llms-full.txt, which carries the full content as markdown.

It is a proposed convention rather than a standard, and no model provider is obliged to read it. It costs about an hour to write. The useful side effect is that writing one forces a company to say plainly what it does and which pages matter.

### Why does brand consistency matter for AI search?

Source: https://bravenewhive.com/ai-marketing/why-brand-consistency-matters-for-ai-search/
Date: 2026-09-01. Read: 3 min.

Because a model reads every version of your company that exists online and averages them. Three different descriptions produce a vague answer or no answer. One description, repeated exactly, produces a sentence the model can quote.

Consistency used to be a design argument about logos and tone of voice. It is now a retrieval argument. The old directory entry, the abandoned profile, the press release from the last positioning, the conference bio written in a hurry: a model weighs all of them alongside the current homepage.

The fix is unglamorous and finite. Write one entity statement, a sentence or two saying what the company is, who it serves and where. Then replace the description everywhere it appears: the site, the schema, every social profile, every directory, every author bio, every partner page.

Marketers resist this because repeating the same sentence feels lazy. It is the opposite. Variation is the part the writer enjoys and the part the machine cannot use.

## 05 Reputation

What a reputation is, how it differs from a brand, how trust is measured, and what the documented cases teach about keeping it.

### Brand versus reputation: what is the difference?

Source: https://bravenewhive.com/reputation/brand-versus-reputation/
Date: 2026-09-14. Read: 3 min.

A brand is what a company says and shows about itself. A reputation is what others conclude from what it does. One is authored, the other is earned, and in a buying meeting the second one decides.

Brand is the set of promises and signals a company controls: its name, its claims, its design, its tone. Reputation is the judgement held by people the company does not control: customers, employees, journalists, regulators, and now the models that read all of them.

The two drift apart when the promise outruns the behaviour. That gap is where crises start, and it is the first thing an institutional buyer checks before signing anything.

### The Edelman Trust Barometer

Source: https://bravenewhive.com/reputation/the-edelman-trust-barometer/
Date: 2026-09-12. Read: 3 min.

An annual survey of trust in business, government, media and NGOs, published by Edelman every year since 2001. It is the most cited public measure of institutional trust.

The barometer surveys tens of thousands of respondents across more than twenty countries each year, and reports trust in the four institutions and in specific sectors. The finding that keeps repeating: business is the institution people trust most, and people expect companies to act on issues governments have not. It measures belief rather than behaviour, which is worth holding on to.

Read the current year's report rather than a summary of it. The numbers move, the headlines about them lag.

### 1982. The Tylenol case

Source: https://bravenewhive.com/reputation/the-tylenol-case-1982/
Date: 2026-09-10. Read: 3 min.

After seven people in the Chicago area died from cyanide-laced Tylenol capsules, Johnson & Johnson recalled the product nationwide and introduced tamper-evident packaging. It remains the reference case in crisis communications.

The company recalled about 31 million bottles, stopped advertising, communicated openly with the press and the public, and relaunched the product in tamper-resistant packaging within months. Market share recovered.

The lesson taught in every crisis course since: act on the public's safety before the balance sheet, say what you know when you know it, and let the packaging carry the promise afterwards.

### What is trust architecture?

Source: https://bravenewhive.com/reputation/trust-architecture/
Date: 2026-09-08. Read: 3 min.

Trust architecture is the deliberate arrangement of proof around a company so that a buyer, a journalist or a model can verify its claims without asking. At Brave New it is the name of that discipline.

Proof is the evidence a claim needs to survive procurement: named clients, audited numbers, dated results, people who can be called. Architecture is putting that proof where it will be found, in the order a sceptical reader checks it.

A brand that asserts and a reputation that is verified are different assets. The second one moves the multiple.

### What is reputation risk?

Source: https://bravenewhive.com/reputation/reputation-risk/
Date: 2026-09-06. Read: 2 min.

Reputation risk is the chance that an event, a decision or a disclosure changes what stakeholders believe about a company, and with it the company's ability to sell, hire, borrow or be regulated on the same terms.

Unlike operational or financial risk it rarely arrives alone. It is the second-order effect of another failure, and it compounds when the company's first statements turn out to be wrong.

The control that works is closing the distance between what a company claims in public and what it can prove on request. A crisis plan in a drawer does much less.

## 06 Readings

Check our readings. The books we like, what each one argues, and one line worth keeping from each.

### How Brands Grow. Byron Sharp (2010)

Source: https://bravenewhive.com/readings/how-brands-grow-byron-sharp/
Date: 2026-09-13. Read: 3 min.

The evidence-based case that brands grow by reaching more buyers, not by deepening loyalty. Built on decades of purchase data from the Ehrenberg-Bass Institute.

> Growth comes from being easy to think of and easy to buy, not from being loved by a few.

Sharp sets out laws that hold across categories: brands with more buyers also have slightly more loyal buyers, most of a brand's sales come from light buyers, and competing brands share customers in proportion to their size. The practical conclusion is mental availability, physical availability and distinctive assets.

It is the book to read before any loyalty programme is proposed. Most of the marketing that feels clever runs against the data in it.

### Ogilvy on Advertising. David Ogilvy (1983)

Source: https://bravenewhive.com/readings/ogilvy-on-advertising/
Date: 2026-09-11. Read: 3 min.

The working manual of the man who built Ogilvy & Mather, on headlines, layouts, research and the difference between advertising that wins awards and advertising that sells.

> The consumer is not a moron. Write as if she were reading over your shoulder.

Ogilvy writes from the agency floor: what he tested, what worked, and what he refused to do. The chapters on headlines, long copy and research are still the plainest instruction on the trade in print.

Read it for the discipline. The examples are old; the standards are not.

### Positioning: The Battle for Your Mind. Al Ries and Jack Trout (1981)

Source: https://bravenewhive.com/readings/positioning-ries-and-trout/
Date: 2026-09-09. Read: 3 min.

The book that moved the battleground from the product to the prospect's mind. Own a word, or a place relative to the leader, before someone else does.

> You do not position a product. You position it in a mind that is already full.

Ries and Trout argue that the mind rejects what does not fit what it already knows, so the job is to find an open position and hold it. Being second is fine if you say so; being a copy of the leader is fatal.

Short, repetitive, and still the origin of the word every strategy deck uses without credit.

### Thinking, Fast and Slow. Daniel Kahneman (2011)

Source: https://bravenewhive.com/readings/thinking-fast-and-slow-kahneman/
Date: 2026-09-07. Read: 4 min.

Kahneman's summary of forty years of research with Amos Tversky on how judgement works in practice: two systems, one fast and automatic, one slow and lazy.

> Most buying is decided before the argument is heard.

The book covers anchoring, loss aversion, framing, the availability heuristic and the planning fallacy, with the experiments that established each. For marketers it is the source text under most of what is sold as neuromarketing.

Long, and worth reading in full once. After that, the Branding section here is the short version.

### The Long and the Short of It. Les Binet and Peter Field (2013)

Source: https://bravenewhive.com/readings/the-long-and-the-short-of-it-binet-field/
Date: 2026-09-05. Read: 2 min.

The IPA study of what produced measurable business effects across hundreds of campaigns: brand building and sales activation work on different timescales and need different creative.

> Activation pays this quarter. Brand pays every quarter after.

Binet and Field analysed the IPA Effectiveness Databank and found that campaigns balancing long-term brand building with short-term activation outperformed campaigns that did either alone. The much-quoted 60 to 40 split comes from here.

A thin report rather than a book, and the most cited document in effectiveness planning.

### Alchemy. Rory Sutherland (2019)

Source: https://bravenewhive.com/readings/alchemy-rory-sutherland/
Date: 2026-09-03. Read: 3 min.

Sutherland's argument that the most valuable ideas in business do not survive a spreadsheet, because people do not choose the way economics assumes they do.

> The opposite of a good idea can also be a good idea.

The book collects cases where a change in perception did the work a change in product could not, and argues for testing the illogical alongside the logical. It is behavioural economics written by a practitioner rather than a professor.

Read it when the plan is rational, complete and somehow not working.

### Influence. Robert Cialdini (1984)

Source: https://bravenewhive.com/readings/influence-cialdini/
Date: 2026-09-01. Read: 3 min.

Cialdini's six principles of persuasion, reciprocity, commitment, social proof, authority, liking and scarcity, each traced to the research and the compliance professionals who use it.

> Every persuasion technique is a shortcut the brain already takes.

The book was written to help people resist persuasion and became the manual for practising it. The chapters on social proof and scarcity explain most of what happens on a landing page.

Later editions add a seventh principle, unity. The original six are enough.

## 07 Research

Original studies from the Hive: how AI engines answer marketing questions, what people type into a search box, and what that means for a brand. Every number comes from a named tool on a stated date.

### How the AI search vocabulary moved in a year

Source: https://bravenewhive.com/research/how-the-ai-search-vocabulary-moved/
Date: 2026-09-14. Read: 4 min.

Three terms for the same worry, tracked month by month. AI marketing spiked and settled, generative engine optimization drifted down from its peak, and answer engine optimization held flat at a lower level.

Method: US monthly search volume for three phrases from Ubersuggest, fetched on 14 September 2026, covering August 2025 to July 2026. The phrases are the three names the market uses for getting a brand into AI answers.

AI marketing is the largest and the most volatile: 9,900 in September 2025, then a slide to 3,600 by May 2026. Generative engine optimization started the period at 6,600 and finished at 4,400. Answer engine optimization never left the 1,900 to 2,900 band.

Reading: the general phrase collects curiosity and then loses it, while the specialist phrases hold a smaller, steadier audience of people who already know what they need. The practical use of that is dull. Put the general name in the title, the specialist names in the headings, and both readers land on the same page.

Limits: one tool, one country, twelve months. We will add other countries and repeat the pull each quarter so the lines get longer.

Figure: How the AI search vocabulary moved. US monthly searches, Aug 2025 to Jul 2026. Source: Ubersuggest, US, fetched 14 Sep 2026. Unit: searches per month.

| Month | AI marketing | Generative engine optimization | Answer engine optimization |
|---|---|---|---|
| Aug 25 | 5,400 | 6,600 | 2,400 |
| Sep 25 | 9,900 | 6,600 | 2,900 |
| Oct 25 | 6,600 | 5,400 | 2,400 |
| Nov 25 | 5,400 | 4,400 | 2,400 |
| Dec 25 | 4,400 | 3,600 | 1,900 |
| Jan 26 | 5,400 | 5,400 | 1,900 |
| Feb 26 | 4,400 | 4,400 | 1,900 |
| Mar 26 | 5,400 | 5,400 | 2,900 |
| Apr 26 | 4,400 | 3,600 | 2,400 |
| May 26 | 3,600 | 3,600 | 2,400 |
| Jun 26 | 3,600 | 3,600 | 2,400 |
| Jul 26 | 3,600 | 4,400 | 2,400 |

### How AI engines answer marketing questions: a citation study

Source: https://bravenewhive.com/research/how-ai-engines-answer-marketing-questions/
Date: 2026-09-14. Read: 5 min.

We asked a live AI engine eight marketing questions and checked every source it named. For six of the eight it never searched, and 21 of the 52 sources it listed do not exist.

Method: eight questions covering marketing principles, the history of advertising, neuromarketing, AI search, films and songs about advertising, marketing reference sites and the term retrievable brand, put to Gemini with Google Search grounding on 14 September 2026, one answer each. Every URL the engine named was requested and its status recorded.

Finding one: live retrieval fired only for the two questions about AI search and marketing reference sites. The evergreen questions were answered from training data, so the sources listed were the model's memory of the web rather than anything it had just read. Twenty-one of fifty-two returned not found. That was the number that surprised us.

Finding two: on the questions where the engine did search, it cited platform vendors, trade publications and several small, recently published explainer posts side by side. A new page can enter those answers within an update cycle. A new page on an evergreen topic cannot, whatever its quality.

What it means: publish the pages on contested, fresh topics first. Treat evergreen reference pages as a search engine play. Verify every citation an engine gives you before repeating it. Limits: one engine, one sample per question. We will repeat the study on other engines and publish the differences.

Figure: Sources an AI engine named, checked one by one. 52 URLs listed across six questions answered without live search. Source: Gemini with Google Search grounding, one answer per question, 14 Sep 2026; each URL requested by hand. Unit: URLs.

| Item | Value |
|---|---|
| Exist | 17 |
| Blocked the check, unverified | 14 |
| Do not exist | 21 |

### What people search for in marketing: the demand map

Source: https://bravenewhive.com/research/what-people-search-for-in-marketing/
Date: 2026-09-14. Read: 4 min.

US monthly search volumes for the topics a marketing reference site might cover. The concept names win, the author names do not, and two categories we planned barely exist as searches.

Method: section names and entry titles for this site were checked in Ubersuggest for US monthly volume and difficulty on 14 September 2026, with short-form demand checked in Virlo over the previous ninety days.

Concept phrasing carries the demand: marketing mix 14,800 searches a month, the 4 Ps of marketing 12,100, market segmentation 9,900, positioning in marketing 9,900, loss aversion 8,100. The same ideas searched by author name get almost nothing: positioning Ries Trout 50, Binet and Field 30.

Category names matter as much. History of advertising draws 720 against history of marketing at 210. Movies about advertising draws 1,300 against movies about marketing at 590. Branding in the age of AI draws 10; AI marketing draws 5,400 and AI SEO 8,100. Songs about marketing draws 70, which is why that section exists for the reader who finds it, not for search.

Short-form video shows the same pattern. The marketing hashtag had 4,234 videos and 140 million views in ninety days; advertising history had six videos averaging 81,000 views each. Demand with almost no supply. We renamed three sections and most entry titles on the strength of numbers like these, which is more deference to a keyword tool than we would usually admit.

Figure: Concept names win, author names do not. US monthly searches for the same idea, two phrasings. Source: Ubersuggest, US, fetched 14 Sep 2026. Unit: searches per month.

| Item | Value |
|---|---|
| Marketing mix | 14,800 |
| 4 Ps of marketing | 12,100 |
| Market segmentation | 9,900 |
| Positioning in marketing | 9,900 |
| Loss aversion | 8,100 |
| Positioning Ries Trout | 50 |
| Binet and Field | 30 |

Figure: Two evergreen topics over a year. US monthly searches, Jul 2025 to Jul 2026. Source: Ubersuggest, US, fetched 14 Sep 2026. Unit: searches per month.

| Month | Neuromarketing | History of advertising |
|---|---|---|
| Jul 25 | 1,300 | 390 |
| Aug 25 | 1,600 | 880 |
| Sep 25 | 2,900 | 1,300 |
| Oct 25 | 2,900 | 880 |
| Nov 25 | 1,900 | 880 |
| Dec 25 | 1,300 | 720 |
| Jan 26 | 1,300 | 880 |
| Feb 26 | 1,900 | 880 |
| Mar 26 | 1,900 | 720 |
| Apr 26 | 1,900 | 720 |
| May 26 | 1,300 | 590 |
| Jun 26 | 1,000 | 390 |
| Jul 26 | 1,900 | 720 |

## 08 Movies about advertising

Films and series about advertising, persuasion, brands and the people who sell them. Year, director and what each one is really about.

### Thank You for Smoking (2005)

Source: https://bravenewhive.com/movies-about-advertising/thank-you-for-smoking/
Date: 2026-09-05. Read: 2 min.

Jason Reitman's satire follows a tobacco lobbyist who can argue any side. A film about spin, and about the difference between persuasion and truth.

Based on Christopher Buckley's 1994 novel. Aaron Eckhart plays Nick Naylor, whose job is to make the indefensible sound reasonable, and who is very good company while he does it. That is the uncomfortable part. Technique works whether or not the claim underneath it is true.

### The Founder (2016)

Source: https://bravenewhive.com/movies-about-advertising/the-founder/
Date: 2026-09-01. Read: 2 min.

Ray Kroc turns a single hamburger stand into McDonald's. The product was the brothers'. The brand, the system and the name became his.

Directed by John Lee Hancock, with Michael Keaton as Kroc. Watch it for one question: what is left of a brand once you separate it from the people who made the product. The film's answer is a name, a set of standards, and the right to sell both.

### Art & Copy (2009)

Source: https://bravenewhive.com/movies-about-advertising/art-and-copy/
Date: 2026-08-28. Read: 2 min.

Doug Pray's documentary on the creative revolution in advertising, with Lee Clow, George Lois, Mary Wells Lawrence, Hal Riney and others on the work that defined the trade.

The film covers Volkswagen's Think Small, Apple's 1984 and Nike's Just Do It, told by the people who made them. It is the clearest record on film of how the modern agency creative department came to be, and the best case we have seen for why it was worth paying for.

### The Greatest Movie Ever Sold (2011)

Source: https://bravenewhive.com/movies-about-advertising/the-greatest-movie-ever-sold/
Date: 2026-08-22. Read: 2 min.

Morgan Spurlock makes a documentary about product placement, funded entirely by product placement. The pitch meetings are the film.

Every sponsor deal, every brand integration and every compromise is on camera. The film shows how brand money shapes content by letting brand money shape it, which is either very honest or very convenient.

### The Century of the Self (2002)

Source: https://bravenewhive.com/movies-about-advertising/the-century-of-the-self/
Date: 2026-08-17. Read: 3 min.

Adam Curtis's four-part BBC series on Edward Bernays and how ideas from psychoanalysis were used to shape public relations, advertising and consumer culture.

Bernays, a nephew of Sigmund Freud, is presented as the link between the unconscious and the business of persuasion. Curtis argues a case rather than reporting one, which is worth knowing going in. It is still the historical backbone of the Branding section, a century before the scanners.

### How to Get Ahead in Advertising (1989)

Source: https://bravenewhive.com/movies-about-advertising/how-to-get-ahead-in-advertising/
Date: 2026-08-11. Read: 2 min.

Bruce Robinson's comedy about an ad executive whose crisis of conscience grows into a talking boil that wants his job.

Richard E. Grant plays Denis Bagley, who cannot finish a campaign for a pimple cream. The film is a satire of the trade from the inside, and one of the few that takes the question of whether advertising is honest work seriously.

### The Joneses (2009)

Source: https://bravenewhive.com/movies-about-advertising/the-joneses/
Date: 2026-08-05. Read: 2 min.

A perfect family moves into a wealthy suburb. They are not a family. They are a stealth marketing unit, and everything they own is for sale.

Derrick Borte's film, with David Duchovny and Demi Moore, got to influencer marketing before the word was common. The neighbours do not buy the products. They buy the life the products are standing in for.

### Mad Men (2007 to 2015)

Source: https://bravenewhive.com/movies-about-advertising/mad-men/
Date: 2026-07-30. Read: 3 min.

Seven seasons of Madison Avenue in the 1960s. The Carousel pitch in the first season is still the best short explanation of what a brand sells.

Matthew Weiner's series follows Don Draper and the agency Sterling Cooper through the decade. The period detail is what people remember. What the show argues, across seven seasons, is that advertising sells the buyer a feeling about themselves rather than a fact about the product.

### Putney Swope (1969)

Source: https://bravenewhive.com/movies-about-advertising/putney-swope/
Date: 2026-07-24. Read: 2 min.

Robert Downey Sr.'s satire: the token Black executive at a Madison Avenue agency is accidentally elected chairman and turns the place upside down.

The film is uneven and deliberately so. It survives because its fake commercials are still funnier and sharper than most real ones.

## 08 Songs

Songs that are about advertising, selling, media and wanting things. Not songs used in ads. Songs about the business of it.

### This Note's for You. Neil Young (1988)

Source: https://bravenewhive.com/songs/this-notes-for-you/
Date: 2026-09-06. Read: 2 min.

A refusal to sell songs to sponsors, with a title that parodies a beer slogan. MTV initially declined to air the video, then gave it Video of the Year in 1989.

The lyric names the brands it will not sing for. The video parodied the celebrity endorsements everyone else was taking. As a statement of the artist's side of the sponsorship bargain, nothing has beaten it since.

### Sell Out. Reel Big Fish (1996)

Source: https://bravenewhive.com/songs/sell-out/
Date: 2026-09-02. Read: 2 min.

A ska-punk band signs to a major label and writes a hit about signing to a major label. The commercial bargain, sung from inside it.

The song knows exactly what it is: the product of the deal it is mocking. That tension is the whole subject of this section, and this song says it out loud.

### Television, the Drug of the Nation. The Disposable Heroes of Hiphoprisy (1992)

Source: https://bravenewhive.com/songs/television-the-drug-of-the-nation/
Date: 2026-08-27. Read: 2 min.

Michael Franti's spoken-word indictment of broadcast media, consumption and attention, written before the feed replaced the channel.

Every line about television reads today as a line about the phone. That it has not dated is a verdict on us, not a compliment to Franti.

### Money. Pink Floyd (1973)

Source: https://bravenewhive.com/songs/money/
Date: 2026-08-21. Read: 2 min.

Cash registers as percussion, a 7/4 riff, and a lyric about the economy of wanting. From The Dark Side of the Moon.

The song became a hit single, which the band found ironic. It sits in this list because wanting is the raw material every marketer works with.

### Material Girl. Madonna (1984)

Source: https://bravenewhive.com/songs/material-girl/
Date: 2026-08-15. Read: 2 min.

Consumer desire as identity, delivered as pop. The video restages Marilyn Monroe's Diamonds Are a Girl's Best Friend.

Madonna has said the song was meant ironically. It became a label anyway, which is the part worth sitting with. The market decided what the brand stood for and did not ask.

### Advertising Space. Robbie Williams (2005)

Source: https://bravenewhive.com/songs/advertising-space/
Date: 2026-08-09. Read: 2 min.

A ballad about Elvis Presley and what fame does to a person once the image becomes inventory.

The title is the thesis. A star's face, name and story become surfaces to sell on. The song is about the cost, sung by someone who knew it.

### Don't Believe the Hype. Public Enemy (1988)

Source: https://bravenewhive.com/songs/dont-believe-the-hype/
Date: 2026-08-03. Read: 2 min.

A song about manufactured media narratives and who gets to write them. From It Takes a Nation of Millions to Hold Us Back.

Chuck D's lyric is a media critique in the form of a hit record. The useful part for marketers is the assumption underneath it: audiences can always tell when a story is being sold to them.

### Radio Radio. Elvis Costello and the Attractions (1978)

Source: https://bravenewhive.com/songs/radio-radio/
Date: 2026-07-28. Read: 2 min.

A protest against commercial radio and the control of what gets heard. Costello famously switched to it mid-performance on Saturday Night Live in 1977.

The song is about gatekeepers deciding what reaches an audience. Replace radio with an algorithm or a model and the argument is current.
